messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Constraints for hierarchical models
parts:
Hi folks,

I'm having trouble figuring out the best way to code models where there is a hierarchical structure on parameters that need to be constrained. The simplest example I could come up with is here:
https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/8119696

In that model, data are generated from a gaussian with mean of zero and standard deviation ("sigma") that is influenced by two variables, "participant" and "condition". There are 100 levels of participant and 2 levels of condition. Sigma values vary across participants according to a gaussian, and the effect of condition on sigma values also varies across participants according to a gaussian. 

Ideally the model should be set up so that it only explores areas of the parameter space that yield positive values for sigma, but despite my efforts thus far, I can't seem to figure out how to achieve this constraint. The result is initialization failure with error messages indicating that some sampled sigma values were negative (ex. "Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[0]  is -2.6257961330947777:0, but must be > 0!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.")

Any suggestions?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints for hierarchical models
parts:
You could always write it as a log-linear model instead of
a linear model --- just exp() transform the linear
predictor.

Your code:

for (i in 1:trialNumTotal)
thisSigma[i] <- personSigma[personNum[i]] + conditionContrast[i] * personSigmaEffect[personNum[i]];

y ~ normal(0, thisSigma);

would change on the second line to this:

y ~ normal(0, exp(thisSigma));

You don't need a Jacobian adjustment for parameter transforms on the
right-hand side of sampling statements.

You can then get rid of all the constraints on the slope
and intercept in the regression for thisSigma.

Alternatively, you could tranform the predictor conditionContrast[i]
if you really want personSigma and personSigmaEffect to be positive.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints for hierarchical models
parts:
Thanks Bob! 

Question on the idea of switching to a log-linear model: if the data are truly generated by a linear-linear process, would the inferences from the log-linear analysis remain valid? For example, since the sigma for a given participant in a given condition is 

    thisSigma[i] = personSigma[personNum[i]] + conditionContrast[i] * personSigmaEffect[personNum[i]]

, if I make the model log-linear by doing "y ~ normal(0, exp(thisSigma));", the previously additive relationship between "personSigma" and "personSigmaEffect" becomes multiplicative, does it not? Doesn't this constitute an inferentially important change in the model?

And a question on the idea of simply recoding the contrasts to avoid negative values: I had them coded as -1/+1 so that it was orthogonal with the intercept; if I recode to +1/+2, is it simply a matter of transforming the samples after sampling to get the original -1/+1 coding back?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints for hierarchical models
parts:
On 12/26/13, 1:26 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Thanks Bob!
>
> Question on the idea of switching to a log-linear model: if the data are truly generated by a linear-linear process,
> would the inferences from the log-linear analysis remain valid? For example, since the sigma for a given participant in
> a given condition is
>
> thisSigma[i] = personSigma[personNum[i]] + conditionContrast[i] * personSigmaEffect[personNum[i]__]

>
> , if I make the model log-linear by doing "y ~ normal(0, exp(thisSigma));", the previously additive relationship between
> "personSigma" and "personSigmaEffect" becomes multiplicative, does it not? Doesn't this constitute an inferentially
> important change in the model?

It's definitely different. Whether it's inferentially important
or not is an empirical question. The linear relationship obviously
doesn't make sense except for values that produce positive scales.

Andrew may jump in here with other advice.

> And a question on the idea of simply recoding the contrasts to avoid negative values: I had them coded as -1/+1 so that
> it was orthogonal with the intercept; if I recode to +1/+2, is it simply a matter of transforming the samples after
> sampling to get the original -1/+1 coding back?

You could translate so the predictor's range is in (0,2), and
then requiring the slope and intercept to be positive will
guarantee the scale is positive. You can translate back, but
that may no longer guarantee positive scales. You need to
invert the linear rescaling, which can be done on the samples.

- Bob
